articles.title: Sonal Dinusha scripts history, breaks Joe Root's all-time 'sweeping' record as Sri Lanka hold India for draw
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sonal Dinusha finished the two-Test series against India with another century and a new Test record, scoring 176 runs through sweep shots, the most by.
articles.body: Sonal Dinusha finished the two-Test series against India with another century and a new Test record, scoring 176 runs through sweep shots, the most by any batter in a Test series.The 25-year-old left-hander remained unbeaten on 133 in Sri Lanka's second innings as the hosts forced a draw in the second Test at the Sinhalese Sports Club in Colombo on Thursday. India still won the two-match series 1-0 after their victory in Galle.Dinusha's unbeaten 133 came after his first-innings 103 in Colombo and his century in the first Test in Galle. It was his third hundred in four innings in the series.According to Cricinfo, Dinusha scored 176 runs through sweep shots across the series. The previous record was held by England's Joe Root, who scored 168 sweep-shot runs against Sri Lanka in 2021.Dinusha also attempted 121 sweep shots during the series, another record for the most sweeps played by a batter in a Test series. Root had attempted 113 sweeps in the 2021 series.After India enforced the follow-on with a first-innings lead of 213 runs, Sri Lanka batted for 243.4 overs across their two innings. Dinusha faced a total of 426 balls in the match.He added 112 runs for the seventh wicket with Keshara Nuwantha, who scored 46, as the pair frustrated India's bowlers on the final day.Sri Lanka resumed Day 5 at 229/6 and continued batting until both teams agreed to end the match with the score at 429/9. Sri Lanka finished with an overall lead of 216 runs.For India, Manav Suthar returned figures of 3/121 in 41 overs, while Ravindra Jadeja took 3/94 in 38.3 overs.Dinusha also became only the sixth batter in Test history to score three centuries in a series while batting at No. 6 or lower. He is the first Sri Lankan to achieve that feat and the first player to do it in a two-match Test series.With his two centuries in Colombo, Dinusha also became only the fifth batter to score hundreds in both innings of a Test while batting at No. 6 or lower. Three of the previous four instances were also by Sri Lankan batters.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The making of Sonal Dinusha: Humble roots and the sweep shot behind Sri Lanka’s new star’s rise
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sonal Dinusha’s twin centuries against India in Galle were the result of much more than a good run of form. The Sri Lankan all-rounder’s remarkable ef.
articles.body: Sonal Dinusha’s twin centuries against India in Galle were the result of much more than a good run of form. The Sri Lankan all-rounder’s remarkable effort in the second Test was built over 13 years of hard work, discipline and the constant backing of a coach who first spotted his potential as a young cricketer.Dinusha scored 103 in Sri Lanka’s first innings and followed it with an unbeaten 133 in the second. His second hundred came after Sri Lanka were forced to follow on, helping them recover from 290 all out and secure a draw and deny India register a 2-0 clean sweep.A boy with a clear visionDinusha grew up in a humble background without the financial resources needed to pursue cricket easily. But from a young age, he showed a determination to make a career in the sport.At the Colombo Cricket Club, coach Sonal Dulshan Alwalage became an important figure in his development. What started as a coach working with a talented youngster eventually became a 13-year project.Dulshan and people around Dinusha helped him continue training when financial limitations could have forced him away from the game. The young cricketer remained focused on his goal and gradually developed into a player capable of competing at the highest level.From spinner to batting starLike many young cricketers, Dinusha initially found his identity as a bowler. He developed into an effective left-arm spinner, but over time it became clear that his batting could take him much further. His development was built around adaptability, technique and an understanding of the game. He learned to assess situations quickly rather than simply attack every ball.One of the clearest examples of that development is his sweep shot.The sweep that became a weaponThe sweep has been one of Dinusha’s most productive strokes, particularly on pitches where spinners play a major role. It is not a shot he discovered after reaching international cricket.He has worked on it since childhood, spending long hours repeating the stroke in the nets. His training sessions could stretch for two to three hours, with the sweep receiving particular attention.That preparation was evident in Galle. Dinusha repeatedly used the shot to counter India’s spinners and turn difficult deliveries into scoring opportunities.Thirteen years of patienceDinusha’s journey to the Sri Lankan team was not sudden. It was built through years of club cricket, training and patience.When his national selection finally arrived, it represented the culmination of more than a decade of work. For Dulshan, who had stayed with him throughout the journey, it was an emotional moment and confirmation that the long-term project had worked.Dinusha also brought leadership experience with him. He became captain of the Colombo Cricket Club, giving him an opportunity to develop his understanding of leading a team.A new chapterDinusha is still only at the beginning of his international career. But his performances against India have offered a glimpse of what years of preparation can produce.The twin centuries were not simply two outstanding innings. They were the latest chapter in a journey that began with a young boy, limited resources, a supportive coach and a clear dream.Thirteen years later, that dream has turned into a Test career — and Dinusha now has the opportunity to build much more.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Blatantly trying to kill him’: Imran Khan’s sons make explosive claims over ex-Pakistan PM prison conditions
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sulaiman Khan and Kasim Khan, the sons of former Pakistan captain and Prime Minister Imran Khan, have expressed serious concern over their father’s he.
articles.body: Sulaiman Khan and Kasim Khan, the sons of former Pakistan captain and Prime Minister Imran Khan, have expressed serious concern over their father’s health and the conditions in which he is being held in prison.Speaking to former England captain and Sky Sports commentator Michael Atherton, the brothers alleged that Imran has been kept in prolonged isolation and has not received adequate medical care. They said they fear for his safety as he approaches three years in prison.Kasim claimed that Imran has suffered a major loss of vision in one eye, estimating that he has lost around 80 per cent of his sight in it. He also said Imran was recently seen wearing an eye patch.According to the brothers, Imran spends more than 23 hours a day alone inside a small cell, with restricted access to books and basic comforts. They also alleged that the cell does not have air conditioning despite the summer heat.“They are not even acting with any kind of strategy any more. It is not very clear what they are doing, just blatantly trying to kill him in there. Keep him in as long as possible, and silence him. The last time he was able to speak to our aunties and anyone else, he said the conditions have severely worsened recently. He has been relating it to other political prisoners who have been killed or who have died in prison. Right now, it is worse than ever, completely isolating him more than 23 hours a day in a cell," Kasim said.Sons fear for Imran’s healthKasim said the priority for the family was now ensuring that Imran receives appropriate medical treatment. He described seeing his father with an eye patch and said the former Pakistan captain appeared visibly stressed.“Right now, it’s really crucial for us that he gets proper treatment. He had an eye patch on for the eye situation, seemed visibly stressed, and that is something that is very hard for us to imagine because he embodies a very calm, assured presence, every time I have ever seen him, including being at gunpoint. A car we were in was robbed, and he was the calmest person there, including the robbers," he added.The brothers also discussed their attempts to travel to Pakistan and visit their father. They claimed their visas had been blocked on technical grounds and said they were willing to accept the possibility of arrest if it gave them an opportunity to see Imran.Sulaiman recalled the family's reaction after Imran was taken for a medical examination following a court order.“We were cautiously optimistic. Our fears were confirmed when, instead of being taken to the private hospital, where he was meant to be taken, he was just taken to a government medical facility for a few hours, and then taken straight back to jail," said Sulaiman.He claimed the examination at the government facility lasted only about an hour and that doctors waiting at Shifa Hospital were not given the opportunity to treat Imran.“In reality, it was an hour check-up by government officials who said, ‘Great, he’s OK’, and then said we will now send him to the independent hospital, Shifa. Instead, they left all the doctors waiting, our auntie waiting, who is a doctor, and sent him straight back to jail," he added.Interview sparks PCB controversyThe interview, which was aired during the lunch break of the second Test between England and Pakistan at Lord’s on Thursday, also created an unexpected controversy involving the PCB.The board lodged a formal complaint with Sky Sports over the broadcast. Reports further suggested that the PCB considered asking Pakistan's players not to return to the field after lunch if the interview was shown.The players eventually returned to the field and the Test continued as scheduled.The interview came shortly after renewed international concern over Imran's medical treatment. He had been taken to a government hospital for a medical examination following a court order relating to his treatment.Former captains back call for medical careThe concerns surrounding Imran have also drawn an appeal from a group of former international captains, including Indian cricket greats Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev.The former captains wrote to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, urging his government to ensure that Imran receives proper medical treatment and humane conditions while in prison.The appeal was framed as a humanitarian intervention rather than a political statement.Imran remains one of the most prominent figures in Pakistan cricket history. He led the country to its first men's ODI World Cup title in 1992 before entering politics and eventually becoming Pakistan's prime minister.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Test cricket won': Shubman Gill after Sri Lanka force draw in Colombo
articles.summary: Following a thrilling second Test match, India captain Shubman Gill hailed the outcome as a victory after Sri Lanka's determined resistance led to a draw. Th...
articles.body:
NEW DELHI: India captain Shubman Gill said "Test cricket won today" after Sri Lanka fought hard to force a draw in the second Test in Colombo on Thursday. India had controlled much of the match and were in a strong position to push for victory. However, Sonal Dinusha produced another outstanding innings, scoring his second century of the match and staying unbeaten as Sri Lanka survived 154 overs. The result saw India finish the two-Test series with a 1-0 victory.

Gill said India made every possible effort during Sri Lanka's long second innings but could not break through their resistance. "We fielded for about 150 overs, we did everything that we can. I don't think we could have done anything differently. Keeping the weather in mind, we could talk about these things (enforcing follow-on) only in hindsight. "You take the best decision you can in the moment and something didn't go our way. But it was a brilliant game and I think Test cricket won today," Gill said after the match here on Thursday. Gill also gave credit to Sri Lanka for their fightback and said India could learn from the way the hosts responded under pressure. "A lot of positives for us, learning from the opposition. The way they came back, it was tremendous to see. I don't think we could have done things differently. They bowled brilliantly in this game."

Gill also spoke highly of left-arm spinner Manav Suthar and backed him to play an important role for India in the future. "How well he releases the ball, I think he's going to be crucial for us in the upcoming years," Gill said.

articles.title: ‘Got to learn from the opposition as well’: Shubman Gill reflects after Sri Lanka deny India clean sweep
articles.summary: Cricket News: India captain Shubman Gill admitted there were plenty of lessons for his side despite the disappointment of missing out on a series clean sweep agains.
articles.body: India captain Shubman Gill admitted there were plenty of lessons for his side despite the disappointment of missing out on a series clean sweep against Sri Lanka, while backing the team to respond strongly when they travel to New Zealand later this year.India had to settle for a draw in the second Test at Colombo after Sri Lanka's lower order produced a determined fightback, led by Sonal Dinusha's unbeaten 133. India still won the two-match series 1-0, but the dropped opportunity to secure another victory affected their World Test Championship points percentage, leaving them fifth in the standings ahead of the New Zealand series beginning on November 19.Speaking in a video by BCCI, Gill said the way Sri Lanka battled over the final three days deserved recognition and felt India could take lessons from their opponents as well."A lot of learnings in this series. I think we played decently well. Obviously not the result that we wanted in this match. After day two, we hoped that it was going to be a win for us, and then Sri Lanka batting the way that they did for these three days. Sometimes you have got to learn from the opposition as well and give credit to them for the way that they played, and hopefully we have a good series in New Zealand."Gill praises Padikkal's impactOne of the biggest positives for India was the form of Devdutt Padikkal, who was named Player of the Series after producing two centuries.With Sai Sudharsan unavailable because of injury, Padikkal made the most of his opportunity and strengthened his case for the No. 3 position in India's Test batting order.Gill was particularly impressed by Padikkal's ability to convert good starts into substantial scores."We speak about once a batsman is set, he should make the most of it, and Devdutt showed that. Very positive signs for us, and the way he batted in the series was a treat to watch, you know, truly tells the mindset of a player, and that is a great positive sign for us," said Gill about Paddikal.Padikkal ended the series as India's leading run-scorer, making 328 runs in three innings at an average of 109.33. His tally included two centuries and a highest score of 167.Across his four Tests and six innings so far, Padikkal has accumulated 418 runs at an average of 69.66, with two centuries and one fifty.Gill identifies Suthar as future spin leaderGill also singled out Manav Suthar for praise after the left-arm spinner emerged as India's leading wicket-taker in the series.Suthar's standout moment came in the first Test at Galle, where he claimed 10 wickets to register the first ten-wicket haul of his career. Gill believes the spinner has the qualities to become a long-term leader of India's spin attack."He has been magnificent for us, and I think he is going to be someone who is going to be leading the spin attack for India for a very long time. And the way he bowled in this match and even in the first match was a treat to watch. Every time he comes on to bowl, it feels like he is going to create those chances and going to get us wickets, and hopefully he keeps doing that," said the skipper.Suthar finished the two-Test series with 16 wickets at an average of 21.06. His haul included a four-wicket spell and a six-wicket haul in the first Test, while his best innings figures were 6/55.Dinusha leads Sri Lanka's fightbackIndia's first-innings total of 503/9 was built around three-figure knocks from Padikkal and Dhruv Jurel.Padikkal made 117 from 193 balls, hitting 12 fours, while Jurel remained unbeaten on 115 from 177 deliveries, with nine fours and two sixes. Rishabh Pant contributed 63 from 89 balls, including six fours and two sixes, while Gill scored 50 from 108 balls with six fours.Asitha Fernando was Sri Lanka's most successful bowler, finishing with four wickets.Sri Lanka responded with 290 in their first innings. Dinusha again played a central role, scoring 103 from 162 balls with eight fours and three sixes. Pasindu Sooriyabandara added a valuable 80 from 133 balls, striking nine fours.Prasidh Krishna and Suthar claimed three wickets apiece for India.Asked to follow on, Sri Lanka were reduced to 218/6 before Dinusha and Keshara Nuwantha launched a stubborn recovery. The pair added 112 runs, with Nuwantha making 46 from 150 balls, including four boundaries.Dinusha completed another century, remaining unbeaten on 133 from 264 deliveries with eight fours and two sixes. His resistance, combined with a lower-order effort that repeatedly frustrated India's bowlers, carried Sri Lanka to 429/9.The draw ended India's hopes of a 2-0 series victory, but Gill believes the experience can prove valuable when India return to Test action in New Zealand in November.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘It takes only one moment of foolishness to lose a Test’: Ashwin’s blunt warning to Rishabh Pant
articles.summary: Cricket News: Ravichandran Ashwin believes Rishabh Pant needs to show greater awareness of match situations and take more responsibility with the bat, despite the w.
articles.body: Ravichandran Ashwin believes Rishabh Pant needs to show greater awareness of match situations and take more responsibility with the bat, despite the wicketkeeper-batter putting together a respectable series against Sri Lanka.Pant finished the two-Test series with 168 runs and two half-centuries. However, Ashwin feels the numbers do not tell the complete story and wants the India batter to exercise more judgement when deciding how to attack.Pant's aggressive approach has come under scrutiny over the past few months, with questions being raised about whether he sometimes takes unnecessary risks and fails to put enough value on his wicket.The former India spinner pointed to Pant's dismissal against South Africa in Guwahati last year as an example. While captaining India in the absence of Shubman Gill, Pant charged down the track against Marco Jansen and edged the delivery to the wicketkeeper.Pant is currently a Test-only player for India after falling out of favour in the white-ball formats. Ashwin believes his decision-making in Test cricket remains an area that needs attention.“My expectation from Rishabh Pant hasn't been fulfilled till now. I am very sorry. Sonal Dinusha had his strike rate up there. But the difference is high-risk options. When you have the game in your hand, these are all statements: ‘That’s how Rishabh plays.' It is about what your team needs,” Ashwin said on ‘Ash Ki Baat’.Ashwin rejects ‘once-in-a-generation’ argumentDuring the discussion, the host argued that Pant's unique ability and his history of producing match-winning performances meant he should be given some freedom to play his natural game.Ashwin, however, insisted that even an exceptional player cannot be exempt from the demands of the situation.“Rishabh played a class knock in Sydney and Brisbane, but you couldn't have won that match without Washington Sundar and Shardul Thakur. It takes 11 cricketers to build a Test and win it in the last session of the game, but it takes only 1 moment of foolishness to lose a Test,” said Ashwin.The former off-spinner clarified that his criticism was not directed at Pant's attacking style itself. Instead, he wants the batter to recognise when the situation demands a different approach.“I am just talking about the times when these chances are being taken when the game is on the line. I love Rishabh the player. It is about playing situations in this format. Sehwag and Gilchrist played high brand of cricket, but these two don't get edged out while dancing down to Marco Jansen when your team is trailing by 500 runs. Don't place these marketing lines in front of me ever again,” he added.Ashwin urges Pant to put team needs ahead of attacking instinctsAshwin also called for more straightforward feedback for Pant, arguing that his status as a special talent should not shield him from criticism.The former India spinner pointed out that Pant has now played 50 Tests and believes his experience means he should be expected to take greater responsibility.“Don't give one player special treatment. This once-in-a-generation player backing, then give it to everyone. Jaiswal is also such a player. All I'm saying, Rishabh, is that he is experienced; he has played 50 Tests. He needs to take responsibility. Don't come up with this ‘once-in-a-generation’ argument. It is because of his decision-making that he's not playing the other two formats. The day you tell him the truth, he will be an all-format player for India,” said Ashwin.Pant's current status outside India's ODI and T20I squads has added further significance to Ashwin's comments. While he remains a key part of India's Test setup, Ashwin believes adapting his approach to different match situations could be the key to Pant eventually returning as an all-format player.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 1139 minutes! How defiant Sonal Dinusha denied India a 2-0 series sweep
articles.summary: Cricket News: TimesofIndia.com in Colombo: 1139 minutes, 722 balls, 420 runs and three hundreds. Over the last two weeks, Sonal Dinusha accumulated staggering numbe.
articles.body: TimesofIndia.com in Colombo: 1139 minutes, 722 balls, 420 runs and three hundreds. Over the last two weeks, Sonal Dinusha accumulated staggering numbers, but the time he spent at the crease will stand the test of time. It was the major reason why Sri Lanka lived to fight on Day 5 in Galle and Colombo against India. Before diving into his heroics, it's important to note his entry points in the four innings against India to add much-needed context.90/4 and 47/4 in the first Test, followed by 122/4 and 209/4 in the second. While the scorecard makes for comfortable reading in the final essay in Colombo, the situation there was the trickiest. Sri Lanka needed to play for time — a lot of it. Two quick wickets in the next few overs meant the 25-year-old was left with just the bowlers for company. He had faced a similar situation in the previous innings, but the stakes were highest on Days 4 and 5 at the SSC, with India desperate for the remaining wickets to enforce a result.Dinusha came with a plan and stuck to it. He made time his closest ally. The support from the other end, coupled with tactical brilliance, meant India toiled for over 86 overs but still couldn't get the result they wanted. He consumed time, scored runs and literally swept India out of the contest on the final day of the Test. The sweep and reverse-sweep were his two strongest shots in the innings that preceded the fourth-innings masterclass, but he looked in maximum control when it mattered most.Shubman Gill was aware of the sweep challenge and covered that region with constant protection for the hit on both sides of the wicket. But it was Dinusha's smart use of footwork that left the visitors clueless throughout the day. Over 40% of his runs in the series came off sweeps, but his control stood out in Colombo. With no vicious bite from the surface and LBW and bowled becoming the least expected modes of dismissal, Dinusha feasted and became only the third batter ever to score twin hundreds in a match where his team was asked to follow on.I thought, jeez, this guy can play. I love the way he plays Test cricket. He thinks about it. He plays to his strengths and he is a smart cricketerDoing it from No.6, with the tail for company, he also became the fifth overall batter to achieve the rare feat.Dinusha's compact game, approach against both spin and pace, and stubbornness made his time against the Indian bowlers difficult throughout the series, establishing him as the best batter across both teams. The number of overs he spent batting with the tail should become an ideal template for batters operating from No.6 and below in the format, which is why his effort attracted plenty of praise from the opposition camp too."He (Dinusha) played really well, his defense was solid, he played some really good sweep shots. And in this match, I don't think there was even a half-chance that he went to a fielder," Gill said while praising the thorn in their flesh."We thought we can get him with pace but there wasn't enough of it on the wicket. Someone like Prasidh was consistently bowling 135-140kmph and bowling bouncers but he was able to defend. So we could see there wasn't enough pace in the wicket to challenge him again and again," he further added.Gill's comments carried an undertone of helplessness, which remained the order of the day before early handshakes brought the curtains down on India's hopes of returning with a 2-0 scoreline. Add to this the frustration of not being able to wrap up the tail quickly in either innings. Over 44 overs in the first innings and then another 90-plus in the second, Dinusha ensured India remained on the park longer than they would have liked. This storyline has continued, with minor adjustments, since Galle."I think it's never easy batting at six in a team because often you come in under pressure. I saw that he really thrives in tough situations. The first time I watched him bat properly was in the first innings in the West Indies," Gary Kirsten said in the post-match press conference."He came in at seven and we were 110 for five and he put on a 100 with the captain (Dhananjaya de Silva)."I thought, jeez, this guy can play. I love the way he plays Test cricket. He thinks about it. He plays to his strengths and he is a smart cricketer," added the veteran coach.There were early butterflies and nervousness in his movements in Galle, but Colombo tasted like different gravy as he gave nothing away and carried the team along in a manner only he could have. In Gill's words, he didn't give a "half a chance", while coach Kirsten quickly termed it one of the "great saves of Sri Lankan Test cricket".The approach remained uncomplicated, allowing him to become only the second batter to have four consecutive scores of 80+; Simon Katich from Australia is the only other batter to achieve the feat, back in 2017. And when he hit Gill's first delivery for a six with the handshake formalities impending, the left-hander could well have murmured to himself — 'keep bowling, I am seeing it like a football now'. He indeed was sighting it better than any other batter, and it wasn't a surprise that he walked away unbeaten, unconquered and the biggest pain for Gill & Co.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1936, Cotar Ramaswami became only second Indian to make Test debut after turning 40; he also played at Wimbledon, disappeared from his home in 1985 and remains listed as ‘death unknown’
articles.summary: Cricket News: Only 13 cricketers in the history of Test cricket have made their debuts after turning 40. Two of them were Indians — Rustomji Jamshedji Dorabji Jamsh.
articles.body: Only 13 cricketers in the history of Test cricket have made their debuts after turning 40. Two of them were Indians — Rustomji Jamshedji Dorabji Jamshedji and Cotar Ramaswami.Jamshedji remains the oldest Indian to make his Test debut. He was 41 years and 27 days old when he played against England in Mumbai on December 15, 1933. Ramaswami, born on June 16, 1896, in Madras (now Chennai), made his Test debut aged 40 years and 39 days against England at Manchester on July 25, 1936.Born on November 18, 1892, in Bombay (now Mumbai), Jamshedji played only one Test for India, while Ramaswami played two.But Ramaswami's story goes beyond his short Test career. He played First-Class cricket for 27 years, represented Cambridge University in tennis and even appeared at Wimbledon. Decades later, he left his home in Chennai one morning and was never seen or heard from again.A family of cricketersCotar Ramaswami was the youngest son of Buchi Babu Naidu, who was a trailblazer in Madras cricket.Ramaswami was a left-handed batter and played 53 First-Class matches, scoring 2,400 runs at 28.91, including two centuries. He also took 30 wickets at 33.06.He came from a family closely connected to cricket. His brothers M Baliah and M Venkataramanjulu played First-Class cricket, as did his son C Ramaswaroop. Four of his nephews and a grand-nephew also played First-Class cricket.Ramaswami made his First-Class debut for Indians against the Europeans in 1915-16. He scored 21 and 31 and took two wickets for 24 runs in the first innings.The following season, in the same fixture, he scored 92 and 44 and took six wickets for 126 runs in the match.The performances caught the attention of the Madras cricket fraternity. However, opportunities were limited. Ramaswami was generally playing only one First-Class match a year and had made just four appearances before leaving for Cambridge in 1919.Tryst with TennisAt Cambridge, Ramaswami continued playing cricket but also took up tennis.He studied there until 1923 and represented Cambridge University in men's doubles. After winning matches during a tour of the Netherlands, he was selected for the Davis Cup team.That year, he also played at Wimbledon.Ramaswami won his first-round match against Britain's Ulysses Williams in a five-set contest, 5-7, 8-10, 6-0, 14-12, 6-3.He was then beaten by Nicolae Misu, who won 6-1, 6-4, 6-3.Back to cricketAfter completing his studies at Cambridge, Ramaswami returned to India and joined the Agricultural Department as an officer.He continued playing cricket for Madras and was part of the first Ranji Trophy match against Mysore, scoring 26.In 1936, at the age of 40, he was selected for India's tour of England.In his book, Ramblings of a games addict, Ramaswami claimed modestly that he was convinced he had been chosen for reasons other than cricket because he had become 'bulky and slow.' His performances on the tour suggested otherwise.He scored 737 runs in First-Class matches at an average of 30.70 before making his Test debut in the second Test at Old Trafford.At 40 years and 37 days, he became the second-oldest Indian to make his Test debut when he received the India cap in the second Test match of the series, at Old Trafford.He scored 40 and 60 in the match, helping India draw the Test. It was also the match in which Vijay Merchant and Mushtaq Ali put together their famous opening partnership of 203 runs.Ramaswami followed that with scores of 29 and 41 not out in the final Test at The Oval.He finished his Test career with 170 runs at an average of 56.66. That was the end of his international career, but Ramaswami continued playing for Madras for several more years.His First-Class career lasted 25 years, during which he scored 2,261 runs at 28.26. He was known as a free-stroking left-handed batter, with a strong drive on both sides of the wicket.He also represented the Hindus in the Bombay Quadrangular and Pentangular tournaments.From player to manager and selectorRamaswami remained involved in cricket after his playing career.He managed India's tour of the West Indies in 1953. The team became one of the most popular Indian sides to visit the Caribbean.In the late 1950s, he became a national selector. The period, however, was marked by disagreements over team selection and India's poor performances.It culminated during the 1958-59 home series against the West Indies, when India had four captains in five Tests and there was considerable disagreement over selection.The disappearanceRamaswami's story took an unexplained turn decades later. On the morning of October 15, 1985, he left his residence in Adyar and never returned.There have been occasional reports of sightings over the years, but none were confirmed.Wisden eventually listed him as `presumed dead'. His whereabouts were never established, although record books later began listing January 1990 as his date of death.Wisden continues to list his death as "death unknown".His family knew little about what happened to him, apart from the fact that he did not want to become a burden on them.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Sri Lanka batter Sonal Dinusha emerged as one of the biggest positives from the drawn two-Test series against India, producing a remarkable display of resilience and consistency to thwart the visitors’ hopes of a series clean sweep.Dinusha scored three centuries across his four innings in the series, finishing as the leading run-scorer with 420 runs at an average of 140.00. He also faced 722 deliveries, the most by any batter in the series, underlining the patience and endurance that made him such a difficult player for India to dislodge.His performance has now earned high praise from former India Test batter Cheteshwar Pujara, who believes the young Sri Lankan has shown glimpses of two of the country's greatest modern-day batters, Kumar Sangakkara and Mahela Jayawardene."The way he has batted throughout the series has been phenomenal. He takes me into that era of batters like Kumar Sangakkara and Mahela Jayawardene. When I was growing up, I used to look up to those Sri Lankan players," Pujara said in a video on ESPNcricinfo.Pujara believes Dinusha has the potential to become one of Sri Lanka's leading batters in the years to come."In five to 10 years, Sonal Dinusha can be one of the greats of Sri Lankan cricket. He has shown that potential. The way he batted on the last day of the second Test match, it was a commendable effort," he added.Dinusha's finest contribution came in the second Test at Colombo, where his unbeaten 133 off 264 balls ensured Sri Lanka held India to a draw and denied the visitors a series clean sweep.How the second match unfoldedComing to the match, India opted to bat first, with centuries from Padikkal (117 in 193 balls, with 12 fours), Dhruv Jurel (115* in 177 balls, with nine fours and two sixes) and half-centuries from Rishabh Pant (63 in 89 balls, with six fours and two sixes) and skipper Gill (50 in 108 balls, with six fours) taking India to 503/9, with Asitha Fernando taking four-fer.In their first innings, SL was skittled out for 290, with Dinusha's second century (103 in 162 balls, with eight fours and three sixes) and a fine 80 from Pasindu Sooriyabandara (in 133 balls, with nine fours) standing out. Dinusha (133* in 264 balls, with eight fours and two sixes) reached his third ton of the series, with the resistance from lower order, who soaked in deliveries to support him. articles.title: The Hundred: Issues caused by competition 'a price worth paying', says Richard Thompson
articles.summary: Scheduling issues caused by The Hundred are a "price worth paying", says England and Wales Cricket Board chair Richard Thompson.
articles.body:
Scheduling issues caused by The Hundred are a "price worth paying", says England and Wales Cricket Board chair Richard Thompson.

The introduction of The Hundred in 2021 squeezed the domestic and international calendar in England, with just two days between the Hundred final and the first Test against Pakistan this summer.

While the ECB has ceded some control to new owners and investors and the addition of future teams remains a possibility, Thompson reiterated the stance that the number of days The Hundred is played across will not grow and said the current positives outweigh the negatives.

"Sacrifices have got to be made," he told Sky Sports.

"If we can take all of the debt out of the game, which we have, make a generation [of counties] which can reinvent themselves, that is a price worth paying."

What has been the impact of new owners on The Hundred?

More than £500m was raised when stakes in the eight Hundred franchises were sold last year - money that has been spread across the professional and domestic game.

Some counties have used the funds to clear debts or invest in infrastructure.

But to maximise the tournament's appeal, a window in July and August has been cleared of international cricket so that England's players are available for their franchises.

England are no longer able to pull their players out of The Hundred to prepare for international matches and bowler Josh Tongue described the turnaround as "crazy scheduling".

"We were criticised that The Hundred finished and two days later we were playing a Test match at Headingley," Thompson said.

"Imagine if that becomes one day - that can't happen."

The Hundred has also added to the congested domestic calendar which includes the County Championship, the T20 Blast and the One-Day Cup, which is now played beneath the Hundred, often as a second-team competition.

"We are having to crowbar so much cricket in," Thompson said.

"There are only four countries in the world that have managed to create a window that can pretty much guarantee the financial success of their game - us, South Africa, India, Australia."

Thompson also described the continued questions around the professionalism of England's men's team as "enormously" disappointing.

Bowler Brydon Carse was left out England's for the second Test against Pakistan after being briefly arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly while on duty with Durham.

He was de-arrested but investigations by the police and Cricket Regulator remain ongoing. Images on social media showed Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers.

"When you play for your country you are judged by far higher standards," Thompson said.

"What comes with wearing those three lions comes with respect, responsibility and pride.

"Unless you live and breathe those qualities there is a problem.

"Every player has to understand the responsibility that comes with playing for England."

articles.title: ‘Treated with the dignity anyone deserves’: Pat Cummins backs campaign for Imran Khan
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: Australia captain Pat Cummins has thrown his support behind a campaign led by former international cricket captains seeking proper medical .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Australia captain Pat Cummins has thrown his support behind a campaign led by former international cricket captains seeking proper medical care and family access for jailed Pakistan great Imran Khan, saying the former all-rounder should be treated with “the dignity anyone deserves”.Cummins, one of the leading active cricketers in world cricket, backed the appeal on Friday after former Australia captain Greg Chappell and 20 other ex-international captains called for Khan to receive humane treatment and independent medical care.“Adding my support here to GC (Greg Chappell) and the other former international captains. I hope the court ordered medical assessment be allowed to run its course, and that family visits continue.“I hope Imran Khan is treated with the dignity anyone deserves,” Cummins posted on X, quoting a short clip of Chappell expressing concerns about Khan’s wellbeing.The intervention makes Cummins one of the first active international cricketers to publicly speak out in support of the campaign surrounding Khan’s medical care.Former captains seek medical care, family accessKhan, 73, has been in custody in Rawalpindi since 2023 after being convicted on corruption charges. He recently underwent a medical examination in Islamabad before being returned to prison.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim, have expressed fears over their father's safety and claimed that attempts are being made to kill him. Cummins echoed the former captains’ call for Khan’s family to continue having access to him.The petition, led by Chappell and addressed to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, has been signed by 21 former international captains, including India greats Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, as well as Sir Alastair Cook, Michael Atherton, Steve Waugh, Adam Gilchrist and Nasser Hussain.The signatories called for a comprehensive health evaluation by a Supreme Court-directed medical board that includes Khan’s personal physicians, uninterrupted weekly family visits and immediate implementation of any recommended treatment.“Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody. Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request,” the letter stated.The former captains described themselves as “former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field” and argued that this bond “transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries”.Chappell raises concerns over Khan’s healthChappell had previously spoken about his concerns during an appearance on The Grade Cricketer podcast, recalling meeting Khan in Pakistan six years ago and describing him then as a “strong, robust older man”.“That’s not the case anymore. His right eye apparently has developed a disability… he’s struggling. He’s been in isolation for three years,” Chappell said.He also described seeing a recent video in which Khan was reportedly taken to hospital in a wheelchair.“He didn’t look well at all. He didn’t look robust. He didn’t look like he could really get around very much,” Chappell said.The former Australia captain also expressed concern about Khan’s reported isolation and its potential impact on his mental and physical health.Khan remains an iconic figure in Pakistan cricket history, having captained the country to its maiden ODI World Cup title in 1992. He later served as Pakistan’s prime minister from 2018 to 2022.Khan has denied wrongdoing and described the cases against him as politically motivated.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: India head coach Gautam Gambhir praised his team for displaying the character and mental strength required in Test cricket after Shubman Gill’s side secured a 1-0 series victory over Sri Lanka. India had a chance to complete a 2-0 sweep after winning the series opener in Galle, but Sri Lanka mounted a spirited fightback in Colombo to force a draw despite being asked to follow on.Gambhir praises India, singles out DinushaFollowing the conclusion of the series, Gambhir took to social media to acknowledge India's performance while also highlighting the impact of Sri Lanka batter Sonal Dinusha."Test cricket needs character, patience and mental toughness that's shown by our boys! Special shoutout to Sonal Dinusha for his exceptional performance," Gambhir wrote on X.Dinusha was the central figure in Sri Lanka's resistance. He scored centuries in both innings of the Colombo Test, including an unbeaten 133 in the second innings, frustrating India's efforts to wrap up the match.Padikkal, Jurel power India to 503India made a dominant start after choosing to bat first in Colombo. Devdutt Padikkal led the charge with a superb 117, while Dhruv Jurel remained unbeaten on 115. Rishabh Pant added 63 and captain Gill contributed 50 as India amassed 503/9 before declaring. Asitha Fernando was Sri Lanka's most successful bowler, finishing with four wickets.Sri Lanka were dismissed for 290 in their first innings, but Dinusha once again stood out with a composed 103. Pasindu Sooriyabandara also played an important role, scoring 80, while India's Prasidh Krishna and Manav Suthar claimed three wickets each. Asked to follow on, Sri Lanka were in serious trouble at 218/6 and India appeared to be closing in on another victory. Dinusha, however, refused to give India an opening.112-run stand changes the game Dinusha joined forces with Keshara Nuwantha to produce a crucial 112-run partnership. Nuwantha's 46 came from 150 deliveries as the pair absorbed pressure and consumed valuable overs. Sri Lanka's lower order then provided further support, allowing Dinusha to remain at the crease until the close.He finished unbeaten on 133 from 264 balls, with eight fours and two sixes, as Sri Lanka reached 429/9 to secure the draw. The result ended India's hopes of a clean sweep but secured them a 1-0 series victory.India had established their series advantage in the opening Test at Galle, where they secured a 165-run victory. articles.title: ‘It’s been lonely, it’s been brutal’: Anaya Bangar opens up on trans journey as Cricket Australia clears path back to cricket
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: For Anaya Bangar, the prospect of returning to competitive cricket is about much more than stepping back onto a field. It represents the cu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For Anaya Bangar, the prospect of returning to competitive cricket is about much more than stepping back onto a field. It represents the culmination of a lonely and emotionally difficult journey that began when she started her transition in 2022.Now on the cusp of reclaiming her cricketing life, the 25-year-old trans athlete says Cricket Australia’s decision to provide her a pathway into women’s cricket is a moment she once thought might never arrive.“It’s been lonely, it’s been brutal, but it’s also been worth it,” Anaya told PTI.Her journey eventually culminated in gender-affirming surgery in March this year. In June, she approached Cricket Australia’s Head of Integrity Jacqui Partridge after learning about the governing body’s policy for transgender and gender-diverse players. The process eventually resulted in CA clearing Anaya for a pathway towards competitive women’s cricket, subject to the policy’s eligibility requirements.“Right now, just hearing the news about Cricket Australia clearing me, and basically providing me a path to play women's cricket, to play cricket as who I am is huge for me,” she said.‘It can get very isolating’Anaya admitted that the transition was an extremely difficult period, particularly while navigating the challenges of being a trans athlete in the current political climate.“...when you're transitioning, and when you're a trans-athlete, during this political climate in this world, it can get very isolating. You feel very lonely, you feel like there's no one who really understands out there,” she said.She found that solitude helped her deal with a situation in which she often felt others were trying to tell her what was best for her.“Everyone out there is trying to give you solutions, when you know that your own case is the right one. You know what is happening with you is injustice. So, during all of this, just the fact of being with myself, solitude has helped me a lot throughout all this,” she added.Anaya, whose father is former India player and decorated coach Sanjay Bangar, said she had eventually given up hope of playing cricket again after beginning her transition.“To be honest, emotionally, it's just been all by myself, but I'm grateful for the support for the necessities that I had from my family,” she said.“I never thought that I'll be able to get (to) play cricket ever since the day I started transitioning. I just tried to put myself out there and see what happens, and whatever works, works. And throughout all this, I think the universe has backed me a lot, and here we are,” she added.‘The experience made me stronger and wiser’Anaya said the experience of stepping away from the sport she loved, undergoing major personal changes and dealing with changing family dynamics ultimately made her stronger.“To be honest, transitioning was always about being happy and comfortable in my own skin. And I had to take the necessary steps during that time in my life to basically give up the sport that I loved. Go through major changes, go through major family dynamic changes and everything,” she said.“...And I couldn't be more grateful for this journey. It's been a rollercoaster, it's been brutal, it's been filled with emotions, but I'm glad I'm on the stepping stone now.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Anaya Bangar has responded to criticism from South Africa all-rounder Marizanne Kapp over her bid to return to competitive women’s cricket, urging those opposed to her participation to “educate themselves” on the subject.Kapp had strongly criticised Cricket Australia’s decision to offer Anaya a pathway back into competitive women’s cricket, calling it “absolutely ridiculous” and saying “this should not be allowed”.The comments came after Cricket Australia cleared Anaya, daughter of former India cricketer and coach Sanjay Bangar, for a pathway towards elite women’s cricket under its Inclusion of Transgender and Gender Diverse Players in Elite Cricket Policy.Anaya, who underwent gender-affirming surgery in March this year, is currently eligible to play community cricket in any state or territory of Australia. Her eligibility for elite cricket from March 2027 remains subject to the policy requirements.Anaya responds to Kapp criticismAnaya’s potential return has generated reactions on both sides, with the 25-year-old now responding directly to Kapp’s criticism.“I think people who want to raise their voice against it should actually educate themselves on this topic, and I've already provided the necessary information in terms of not having any unfair advantage, and also complying with the guidelines set by Cricket Australia.“If anyone's personal opinion is in that sort of way, I hope they go and educate themselves,” she said with a shrug while speaking to PTI.Anaya is hoping to eventually pursue a pathway to the Women’s Big Bash League, although she is yet to sign up with a local club. Her immediate focus is on playing at the community level and proving herself through her performances.‘Baby steps from here’Anaya said she had spent a long period in “survival mode” and was only now beginning to process everything she had experienced during her transition and the long road back to cricket.“...basically now, the next role is to go there and play club cricket and prove myself by my performances, and if I do well, I hopefully might have a chance to be picked for the Women's Big Bash League. So, baby steps from here, but the major part of having a place to play has been cleared,” she said.She is currently in talks with a few cricket clubs and is waiting to decide on the right one “to go there and start playing.”For Anaya, the CA decision represents a significant breakthrough after years away from competitive cricket. While she has been given a pathway, it does not guarantee selection in any team.Anaya further added that the process was neither “automatic or informal”, with CA considering her medical and surgical history, hormone and testosterone levels, cricketing background, playing footage and scientific and athletic performance work undertaken with Manchester Metropolitan University’s Institute of Sport.She also said her most recent blood test in July recorded total testosterone at 0.6 nanomoles, which she said was within the female reference range reported by the laboratory.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ECB chair Richard Thompson 'extremely disappointed' at England cricket off-field incidents
articles.summary: Brydon Carse episode outside a Derby nightclub latest off-field issue for England to manage after Harry Brook being punched by a bouncer, Ben Duckett video in Noosa and Gus Atkinson and Ben Stokes breaking curfew earlier this summer; Joe Root "hacked off" with team's "stupid mistakes"
articles.body:
Fast bowler Brydon Carse was dropped for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's as the Cricket Regulator examines an incident outside a Derby nightclub last weekend.

The Carse situation follows Harry Brook being punched by a bouncer in New Zealand last year, Ben Duckett videoed seemingly drunk in Noosa during The Ashes, and Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson breaking curfew to attend a London nightspot this summer.

New captain Joe Root, who has taken over from the retired Stokes, said he was "hacked off" by England continuing to make "stupid mistakes" when speaking to the media earlier this week.

'Every player has to understand responsibility of playing for England'

Thompson said to Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton on Friday morning: "I don't think anyone could have summed it up better than Joe [Root] did this week.

"When you play for your country, you are judged by a far higher standard. What comes with wearing the three lions comes with respect, responsibility and pride.

"Unless you live and breathe those three qualities, there's a problem. I think every player, and Joe articulated this brilliantly, has to understand the responsibility that comes with playing for England."

Speaking about the Carse story at Lord's on Thursday, Sky Sports pundit and former England seamer Stuart Broad said: "Carse is in a very worrying situation because Root is now in charge. It's a fresh page. Joe can say, 'this is my team, this is what we are doing'.

"When you are getting reprimanded by the Cricket Regulator or the ECB, you don't know who that is, but when Root says, 'I expect this from you and if you don't deliver that we have a problem', then you are not crossing Root.

"That is the strong position Root is in after what he has said to the group - players will start to behave.

"I thought what Root said in the press conference was very strong and what an opportunity for him to say, 'this is my team and we will do it my way'."

Thompson: England wanted to be 'measured' after Ashes

Root will work alongside new Test coach Stephen Fleming moving forward with the latter succeeding fellow New Zealander Brendon McCullum in the role.

Fleming's first assignment will be a three-match series in South Africa over the winter, with Marcus Trescothick in interim charge against Pakistan.

McCullum was axed following the 2-1 home defeat to New Zealand in June, having presided over seven defeats and just two wins in England's previous nine Tests.

Asked why change did not come after the error-strewn 4-1 Ashes thrashing in Australia this winter, Thompson added: "We all wanted to be very considered.

"When you lose 4-1, the expectation is that heads will roll. That's what's always happened before. The reality is when you lose an Ashes, a number of people lose their jobs.

"You learn nothing from it. You never get the chance to learn what those lessons were, and you never get to understand what those lessons are and put them right.

"Within days of the Ashes finishing, we were also going into a Sri Lanka white-ball tour and an important T20 World Cup with the same coaching group and players.

"That's the reality of modern cricket; being swift is hard when you are back-to-back with tournaments.

"The reality was we wanted to be measured. We felt that there were lessons that could and should have been learned."

articles.title: Dewald Brevis’ 75 runs goes in vain as Namibia beat South Africa by 18 runs in tri-series opener
articles.summary: Cricket News: Namibia produced another memorable upset against South Africa, defending 163/9 to secure an 18-run victory in the opening match of the Namibia T20I Tr.
articles.body: Namibia produced another memorable upset against South Africa, defending 163/9 to secure an 18-run victory in the opening match of the Namibia T20I Tri-Series 2026 at the Namibia Cricket Ground on Friday. It was Namibia's second win over South Africa in 10 months, underlining their growing stature in the shortest format. The hosts appeared to have left the door open after South Africa restricted them to 163, but their bowlers responded brilliantly to dismiss the Proteas for 145/9 in 20 overs.Dewald Brevis produced a superb 75 off 50 balls, but his valiant effort could not take South Africa over the line. Ruben Trumpelmann and JJ Smit claimed three wickets apiece to lead Namibia's bowling attack.Frylinck, Steenkamp provide perfect startAsked to bat first, Namibia made an explosive start through Jan Frylinck and Louren Steenkamp. The opening pair put together an 84-run partnership, giving the hosts the platform they needed to post a competitive total.Frylinck was particularly impressive, striking 60 off 38 balls with six fours and two sixes. Steenkamp complemented him perfectly with a brisk 41 off 29 deliveries. Namibia appeared set for a much bigger total when they reached 133/3 in the 15th over, but South Africa hit back strongly during the final five overs.The Proteas' bowlers suddenly found their rhythm and picked up six wickets for just 30 runs in the final five overs. Prenelan Subrayen led the fightback with 3/32, while captain Bjorn Fortuin bowled a disciplined spell to finish with 2/17.The late collapse prevented Namibia from reaching what could have been a significantly higher score, with the hosts eventually finishing on 163/9. South Africa therefore needed 164 to begin the tri-series with a victory.Namibia pacers rattle ProteasThe chase began poorly for South Africa as Namibia's seamers immediately applied pressure. Trumpelmann was particularly effective, using his left-arm angle to trouble the Proteas' top order. He eventually finished with 3/24, while Smit provided excellent support with 3/31.South Africa's young batting line-up struggled to build partnerships, leaving Brevis with the responsibility of keeping the chase alive. Brevis responded with a magnificent counter-attacking innings.The right-hander scored 75 from 50 balls, including five sixes, and repeatedly found boundaries to keep South Africa within touching distance of the target.With wickets falling around him, Brevis continued to attack and appeared capable of taking the Proteas close to victory. But his dismissal in the 18th over effectively ended South Africa's hopes.Duan Jansen provided a late push with 25 off 17 balls, but Namibia's bowlers held their nerve during the closing overs.With the required rate climbing and wickets running out, South Africa finished on 145/9, 18 runs short of the target.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Sarah Taylor: England fielding coach says role has been 'strange' but 'amazing' and enjoying working with Jamie Smith
articles.summary: Sarah Taylor first woman to coach an England men's side in a major sport; former wicketkeeper played 226 internationals for England women between 2006-2019; Taylor enjoying watching wicketkeepers standing up to the seam bowlers in Test cricket and says it allows them to show their skills
articles.body:
Former England women's player Taylor, regarded as one of the best wicketkeepers the game has seen, began her role with the senior men's side team this summer, following coaching stints with England Lions, Sussex and in The Hundred.

The 37-year-old is the first woman to coach an England men's side in a major sport.

Speaking to Sky Sports Cricket's Ian Ward prior to day two of the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's, Taylor said of her job: "It is a bit strange but what's brilliant about these guys is that they just call me coach.

"That's exactly what you want. I am entering their space so I have to respect their space. I have genuinely loved it, felt so welcome.

"It has been a normal transition into the Lions set-up and then this set-up. The boys have been amazing and I cannot complain at all."

'Smith is a project and knows what he needs to do'

Smith's glovework has been largely immaculate this summer, with the Surrey man often asked to move up to the stumps to the seamers, a trend in the global game and one Australia and New Zealand have deployed against England in recent series.

Taylor said of the England wicketkeeper: "Jamie has been very clear on what he wants to achieve and where he wants to go with his keeping. He is a project and he knows what he needs to do.

"It is just little tinkering changes here and there. His stood-up stuff has definitely improved and his movement as well.

"We get on extremely well and clicked straightaway, which is a blessing as a coach. I have loved it, it has been an absolute dream."

On wicketkeepers coming up to the stumps more generally, Taylor added: "A few years ago the wicketkeeper standing up was a punch to a bowler's ego, whereas now it is seen as a real positive.

"You are trying to enhance those bowlers' skills, especially when the ball is nipping around and the wicket is helpful for that.

"Wicketkeepers have to get better at that, especially against the speed they are facing.

"Ultimately, that's what Jamie has been working extremely hard on - staying a lot more still, especially with the moving ball.

"Watching some of the wicketkeepers, they are really showing their true skill that they weren't able to show as much before.

articles.title: The Netherlands beat Scotland women by 58 runs in first of three ODIs
articles.summary: The Netherlands comfortably beat a youthful Scotland side to take the lead in a three-match ODI series.
articles.body:
Netherlands 270-4 (50 overs): Molkenboer 106, De Leede 69; Maqsood 1-35

Scotland 212-10 (48.5 overs): Sproul 79, McColl 33; Siegers 3-42

The Netherlands comfortably beat a youthful Scotland side to take the lead in a three-match ODI series.

Having won the toss, stand-in Scotland captain Abtaha Maqsood opted to bowl at Clydesdale Cricket Club but the hosts struggled to make inroads on a good pitch.

Maqsood dismissed Sanya Khurana for 46 to get Scotland on the board. However, fellow opener Phebe Molkenboer amassed a superb 106 - her first ODI hundred - as the Dutch set 270-4 in their 50 overs.

Babette de Leede made 69 and Robine Rijke 18 in an impressive batting effort.

Without the likes of key players Kathryn and Sarah Bryce, Kirstie Gordon and Katherine Fraser, Scotland handed debuts to Charlotte Nevard and Rebecca McCrossan.

However, both failed with the bat in their first international outings as Nevard was trapped lbw first ball by Caroline de Lange and McCrossan was bowled by Khurana for five.

Hampshire wicketkeeper Pippa Sproul made 79 but Scotland fell 58 short of their target.

The next two fixtures are on Sunday and Tuesday, both at Stirling County Cricket Club.

The series was arranged at short notice as the Netherlands seek to regain their ODI ranking and avoid a substantial funding cut next year.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer give hosts control at Lord's
articles.summary: England’s quartet of seamers once again overwhelm Pakistan to put the home side on the verge of a series win on the second day of the second Test at Lord’s.
articles.body:
Second Rothesay Test, Lord's (day two of five)

England 290 (Smith 61, Cox 55; Abbas 4-73) & 81-3 (Gay 30*)

Pakistan 110 (Awais 46; Robinson 4-11, Archer 3-26)

England's quartet of seamers once again overwhelmed Pakistan to put the home side on the verge of a series win on the second day of the second Test at Lord's.

Led by Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer, and supported by Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson, the foursome gave another demonstration of why there is growing optimism around the England attack.

The struggling Pakistanis, without the injured Imam-ul-Haq, were hustled out for 110. Only Azan Awais, who made 46, passed 20 – extras was the next highest score.

Robinson continued his sensational comeback summer with 4-11, while Archer bowled with electrifying pace for his 3-26.

It gave England, who earlier extended their first innings to 290, an advantage of 180 runs.

The hosts were soon 13-2 in their second innings before being steadied by a stand of 47 between Emilio Gay and Joe Root.

As the light drew in, Root was dismissed by Mohammad Ali for 24, the captain once again lbw to a seam bowler in what has become a trend for England's all-time leading run-scorer.

Harry Brook overturned being given out lbw first ball to the same bowler and Gay battled to 30 not out. The opener has the opportunity for a much-needed score to quieten questions about his place in the side.

England reached 81-3, a lead of 261. Given Saturday's weather forecast, they may have to wait some time to build their advantage.

England battle to commanding lead over Pakistan - day two as it happened

If a competitive first day, when England reached 248-9, left this match evenly poised, the second day was almost entirely dominated by the home side and put them in complete control.

Atkinson and Tongue added 42 runs on Friday morning to take their 10th-wicket partnership to 47. It gave England all the momentum.

And the value of England's total was put into context by the quality of their bowling. Batting conditions eased slightly on day two, though there was still plenty of assistance for bowlers who put the ball in the right place. England were relentless in doing so again and again.

Pakistan were unfortunate to lose opener Imam to a calf injury, but his absence probably did little to alter the outcome.

Even with England's wobble at the beginning of their second innings, they probably already have enough to win this match and the series. In three attempts so far on the tour, Pakistan's highest total is 171 and they have not managed to bat for 50 overs.

Saturday's weather forecast is horrendous, possibly a complete washout. If that is the case, England still have more than enough time to wrap up victory over the bank holiday weekend.

Electrifying Archer and relentless Robinson

England's pace attack has come together out of necessity following the retirement of Ben Stokes. Excitement over its future prospects should be tempered because of the fragility of the opposition, yet there is no doubt England's bowlers have been outstanding so far in this series.

Archer, as he often is at Lord's, was sensational and deserved more. His top speed in a terrifying opening spell touched 95mph and he averaged 90.7mph.

Somehow, with Awais constantly playing and missing, the only victim in Archer's first five overs was Shan Masood.

Robinson was a complete contrast yet no less effective. Operating almost exclusively with wicketkeeper Jamie Smith up to the stumps – Smith was magnificent - Robinson barely reached 80mph. Still, he gave the batters a forensic examination with metronomic accuracy and exaggerated movement in the air and off the seam.

Behind them, Tongue's full length gave him two wickets – Tongue has struck once every 13.3 balls in this series. Somehow, Atkinson has taken only one wicket in three innings and was denied another when Awais reviewed being given caught behind, a decision overturned as the players were leaving the field for a short rain delay.

When they returned, Robinson and Archer were irresistible. Two smart lbw reviews to remove Saud Shakeel and Muhammad Rizwan, followed by a short ball to get Awais, took Robinson's tally this summer to 19 wickets in three matches at an average of 8.84.

Archer got some overdue rewards by bowling both Ali Usman and Muhammad Abbas. His bowling average on this ground is 17, compared to more than 30 everywhere else.

England's top order is becoming congested. Jordan Cox has two half-centuries in this series and someone may have to be squeezed out when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury. Gay has given himself the chance to ensure it will not be him.

The home side were two down inside 19 balls. Ben Duckett played an awful drive to be caught at mid-off and Cox was trapped on the crease to be lbw, both to Khurram Shahzad. Given their healthy lead, there was no panic for England, but caution was required.

Left-hander Gay was patient, occasionally scoring through the off side. Root looked to have played himself in, only to again find himself pinned on the pad.

When Ali nipped one back to Root, the captain reviewed in desperation. This was the ninth time in seven Tests he has been lbw to a seam bowler, having fallen in similar fashion only three times in his previous 39 matches. It is a problem whether the wicketkeeper is standing up to the stumps or not.

The next ball, to Brook, was almost identical. The England vice-captain was spared the same fate as Root thanks to an inside edge.

The light faded quickly and batting became about surviving to the oncoming close. Gay survived an edge off Abbas that did not carry and now has an opportunity he must take.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer skittle visitors as Joe Root's side take 261-run lead in second Test
articles.summary: Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer rattled their way through Pakistan's batting order as England took a 261-run lead on day two of the second Test at Lord's.
articles.body:
England's bowlers excelled with both the ball and the bat, as the hosts started the day with Josh Tongue (30no) and Gus Atkinson (45) at the crease.

The tailenders set the tone early, moving England to a first-innings score of 290, thanks to their 47-run stand, before the hosts' fiery bowling attack returned to the field to skittle Pakistan for 110 runs inside 37.2 overs.

Back at his happy hunting ground of Lord's, Robinson, who took a haul of seven wickets here against New Zealand in June, was the pick of England's bowlers with impressive figures of 4-11.

England returned to the field after tea, but lost wickets quickly, with Ben Duckett (1), Jordan Cox (11), and Joe Root (24) all falling inside 16 overs.

Play was abandoned at 6.50pm due to bad light, with England 81-3 at stumps, with Gay (30) and Harry Brook (7) set to return to the crease on Saturday morning.
